title: Named groups and numbering
summary: Give groups names so code survives pattern edits, the .NET numbering rule that differs from JavaScript and Python, ExplicitCapture, replacements with ${name}, and extracting fields on the command line.

steps.title: Named groups: (?<name>...)
body: `m.Groups[3]` tells a reader nothing, and it silently changes meaning when someone adds a group earlier in the
pattern. Give the group a name instead:
```csharp fragment
var m = Regex.Match(line, @"(?<level>[A-Z]+) \[(?<svc>[\w-]+)\] (?<msg>.*)");
if (m.Success)
Console.WriteLine($"{m.Groups["svc"].Value}: {m.Groups["level"].Value}");
In a replacement, refer to a named group with `${name}`, and to a numbered one with `$1` or `${1}`. Use the
braces when a digit follows: `${1}0` is group 1 and then a zero, but `$10` means group 10.
Below, the replacement reorders the fields by name.

steps.title: A date with named parts
prompt: Match the whole string when it is an ISO date like `2026-11-26`, and name the parts: `y` for the four-digit year,
`m` for the two-digit month, `d` for the two-digit day. ASCII digits only.
hints: A named group is `(?<y>...)`. The year is `[0-9]{4}`.
steps.explain: The checks read the groups by name. This pattern checks the shape only: `2026-13-45` passes. Validate the values with `DateOnly.TryParseExact` after the match.

steps.title: The .NET numbering rule
body: Named groups also have numbers, and here .NET differs from almost everyone else.
- **.NET**: unnamed groups are numbered first, left to right. Named groups come **after** them, in order.
- **JavaScript, Python, PCRE, Java**: every capturing group is numbered left to right, named or not.
```text
pattern:  (?<level>[A-Z]+) (\d+) (?<svc>\w+)
.NET:     1 = (\d+)     2 = level   3 = svc
JS/Py:    1 = level     2 = (\d+)   3 = svc
So a pattern ported from Python with `$1` in the replacement can silently insert the wrong field in C#. The cure
is to not mix the two styles: name every group you read, and make the rest `(?:...)`.
**`RegexOptions.ExplicitCapture`** (flag `n`, or `(?n)` at the start of the pattern) does that for you: plain
`(...)` stops capturing, and only named groups capture. Then `Groups[1]` is the first named group.

steps.prompt: Remember the .NET rule. What does this print?
steps.explain: The only unnamed group, `(\d+)`, is number 1. Then the named groups follow in order: `level` is 2, `svc` is 3. In JavaScript or Python, group 1 would be `ERROR`.

options: an empty string: group 1 does not exist
It throws: ExplicitCapture forbids plain parentheses
steps.explain: With ExplicitCapture, `(\d+)` only groups. The only capturing group is `id`, so it is number 1 (and `m.Groups["id"]` works as usual).

steps.title: Symptom: the latency dashboard shows status codes
prompt: **Symptom.** Since Tuesday's deploy, the p95 latency chart shows values like 200 and 503 milliseconds, and the
alert for slow requests never fires. Nothing in the chart code changed.
The parser below used to have the pattern `(\S+) (\d{3}) (\d+)ms`, where group 3 was the latency. On Tuesday a
teammate added the method group at the front so another report could read it.
Find the cause, then fix it so the next edit to the pattern cannot break it again: **name the groups and read
them by name**. `LatencyMs` returns the milliseconds, or `null` for a line that does not fit.
starter: // Tuesday: added (GET|POST) at the front for the method report.
template: Dojo.Eq("a line without a latency gives null", (int?)null, LatencyMs("starting worker"));

forbid.message: Reads groups by name, not by number

hints: Count the groups: adding `(GET|POST)` in front shifted every number by one. Group 3 is now the status code.
Write `(?<ms>\d+)ms` and read `m.Groups["ms"].Value`. Naming the other groups too keeps them readable.
steps.explain: A numbered group is a position, and positions move when the pattern changes. A name moves with its group. In review, treat a new group inserted before `Groups[n]` reads as a breaking change.

steps.title: Reformat dates with a named replacement
prompt: A report needs dates as `day/month/year`. Write a pattern that finds ISO dates like `2026-11-26` with named groups
`y`, `m` and `d`, and a replacement that rewrites them as `26/11/2026`. Text around the dates stays as it is.
hints: The pattern is the one from the earlier step. In the replacement, `${d}` inserts the day.
steps.explain: `Regex.Replace(text, pattern, "${d}/${m}/${y}")` does the whole file in one call. Named references in the replacement survive pattern edits for the same reason named reads do.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: pulling fields out of text
steps.body: When you need one field from thousands of log lines, print just the capture and pipe it on to sort, uniq or a spreadsheet.

toolkit.what: Print only what group 1 captured, one per line. rg supports named groups too: -r '$user' with (?P<user>...) or (?<user>...).
flags: print only the matched part, not the whole line
replace the output with this template; $1 or $name is a group
drop the file name in front of each hit
toolkit.example: rg -o -N --no-filename -r '$1' 'user=(\w+)' logs/ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
toolkit.when: which users, ids or endpoints show up most in a log

toolkit.what: GNU grep with PCRE. \K throws away what was matched so far, so -o prints only the part after it. No group needed.
flags: Perl-compatible regex (GNU grep; macOS grep has no -P)
keep only the text matched after this point
toolkit.example: kubectl logs deploy/checkout --since=1h | grep -oP 'order_id=\K\d+' | sort -u | wc -l
toolkit.when: on a server or in a container where rg is not installed

toolkit.what: Rewrite with groups. -E gives modern syntax, so ( ) group without backslashes, and \1 inserts a group in the replacement.
flags: sed has no \d: write the class
toolkit.when: a quick rewrite in a CI script or a Dockerfile

toolkit.what: PowerShell's -match uses .NET regex and fills the automatic $Matches hashtable with the groups of the match.
flags: a named group; $Matches[1] for a numbered one
toolkit.when: on Windows servers and build agents

toolkit.what: In C#, the regex source generator turns the pattern into code at build time: no parsing at startup, and a bad pattern is a compile error.
flags: on a static partial method (or, since .NET 9, a partial property) returning Regex
a timeout, for input you do not control
toolkit.when: any pattern used on a hot path in a service

steps.prompt: Match each piece of syntax to what it does.
pairs: print only group 1 of each match
forget what was matched so far
a named group in a .NET replacement
steps.explain: Every tool can print or reuse a group; only the spelling changes. sed and grep use `\1`, .NET, rg and JavaScript use `$1`.

steps.prompt: Complete the command: list the ten most common endpoints in the access logs, printing only the captured path.
code: rg __1__ -N --no-filename __2__ '$1' '"GET (/[^ ?"]*)' logs/ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.explain: `-o` prints only the match, and `-r '$1'` replaces it with group 1, the path. `-F` would turn off the regex, so the group would not exist.

steps.title: Parse a log line into a record
prompt: Lines from the checkout service look like this:
```text
09:12:04 ERROR [checkout] 503 payment declined
A time, a level (capital letters), a service in square brackets (letters, digits and dashes), a three-digit
status, and the rest of the line as the message.
Write `LogEntry? ParseLog(string line)` that returns a `LogEntry` for a line that fits **the whole format**, and
`null` for any other line. The record is already declared:
```csharp
record LogEntry(string Time, string Level, string Service, int Status, string Message);
Use **named groups** and read them by name. `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("an ERROR line", new LogEntry("09:12:04", "ERROR", "checkout", 503, "payment declined"), ParseLog("09:12:04 ERROR [checkout] 503 payment declined"));
Dojo.Eq("a service name with a dash", new LogEntry("09:13:00", "INFO", "order-api", 200, "ok"), ParseLog("09:13:00 INFO [order-api] 200 ok"));
Dojo.Eq("a message with brackets in it", new LogEntry("09:14:10", "WARN", "pay", 429, "retry [2/5]"), ParseLog("09:14:10 WARN [pay] 429 retry [2/5]"));
Dojo.Eq("a line that does not fit gives null", (LogEntry?)null, ParseLog("starting up..."));
Dojo.Eq("a four-digit status gives null", (LogEntry?)null, ParseLog("09:15:00 WARN [checkout] 5030 slow"));
Dojo.Eq("text before the time gives null", (LogEntry?)null, ParseLog("> 09:12:04 ERROR [checkout] 503 payment declined"));
record LogEntry(string Time, string Level, string Service, int Status, string Message);

forbid.message: Reads groups by name, not by number

hints: Anchor both ends with `^` and `$` so a line that only partly fits is rejected. The service is `\[(?<svc>[\w-]+)\]`.
After `if (!m.Success) return null;`, build `new LogEntry(m.Groups["time"].Value, ..., int.Parse(m.Groups["status"].Value), m.Groups["msg"].Value)`.
